title: There is no largest prime, and the proof is over 2,000 years old
body: Primes, numbers divisible only by 1 and themselves, get rarer as numbers grow, so you might expect them to run out eventually. Euclid showed in his Elements, written around 300 BC, that they never do. His argument is short enough to explain in a minute, it’s still taught today, and mathematicians have since found at least 200 different proofs of the same fact.

slides.heading: Share of whole numbers that are prime, up to each limit
slides.note: 4 of the first 10 numbers are prime, 25 of the first 100, 78,498 of the first million.

slides.heading: Take any list of primes
slides.text: Suppose you have a finite list of primes, say 2, 3 and 5. Multiply them all together and add 1: 2 × 3 × 5 + 1 = 31.

slides.heading: Nothing on it divides
slides.text: The new number leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by any prime on your list, so none of them can be a factor of it.

slides.heading: So a prime is missing
slides.text: It must be prime itself or have a prime factor that isn’t on your list. Either way the list was incomplete, whatever list you started with.

slides.heading: A common mix-up
slides.text: The new number isn’t always prime: 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 + 1 = 30,031 = 59 × 509. But 59 and 509 are primes missing from the list.

slides.question: Multiply every prime on a list together and add 1. Why can’t any prime on the list divide the result?
options: It always leaves a remainder of 1
The list is always too short
slides.explanation: Dividing by any prime on the list leaves a remainder of 1, so none of them is a factor. The result is either prime itself or has a prime factor missing from the list.

slides.heading: Which one is not prime?
slides.explanation: 30,031 = 59 × 509. The other three are prime: 31 = 2 × 3 × 5 + 1 happens to be prime, but a product of primes plus one need not be.
